lesson.title: Cloud-native and disaggregated DBMSs: locality becomes a protocol
lesson.short: Compute/storage separation · ownership · logging · failure recovery
lesson.timeMeaning: Suggested independent study minutes; not scheduled contact time
lesson.lead: Separating resources makes scaling more flexible. It also moves familiar memory and recovery decisions across a network.
goals: Compare shared-nothing, shared-storage and compute-memory-storage designs.
Trace page ownership, write-ahead logging and recovery responsibilities.
Estimate remote-access costs and design a workload/failure experiment.

sections.title: Start here: prerequisites and course status
sections.html:
A client received “commit successful,” then the compute node failed before its modified page reached storage. Another node reads an older page. Where can the acknowledged change be recovered? We will follow that one page before drawing a cloud architecture.

Recall buffer management, concurrency and recovery from lessons 5 and 19–22. The numerical and protocol traces are original simplified examples, not the exact implementation of any named system. This supplemental practice is not an Edinburgh lecture or verified Canvas assignment; assigned readings, assessment rules, deadlines and submission arrangements remain unverified.

sections.title: Draw the resource and responsibility boundaries
sections.html:
First put compute, cached pages and durable state on paper. In a shared-nothing design, each worker owns a partition and its local resources; cross-partition operations communicate. Separating compute from storage lets compute nodes access a durable storage service. A further memory service can hold shared buffers or coordination state independently of compute.

Why separate them? We may want more compute without copying the entire durable dataset, or more storage without buying the same compute ratio. But a new compute node has a cold cache. Reads may now cross a network; membership, routing and ownership still need coordination. “Serverless” hides some operations from the user, not the servers or their failure modes.

For every box, label owned state, replication, consistency and failure behavior. A cache is not automatically authoritative, and authoritative state is not automatically durable. CXL memory expansion and network RDMA are different mechanisms; drawing a remote-memory box does not specify either protocol. These distinctions let us ask precisely where an update survives.

Key takeaway

Independent scaling does not imply independent correctness. Coordination and durability contracts still connect the layers.

sections.title: Worked example: latency, bandwidth and caching
sections.html:
A query needs 1,000 remote pages of 8 KiB each: 1,000×8,192=8,192,000 bytes. At an assumed usable 2 GiB/s, transfer time alone is 8,192,000/(2×1,073,741,824)≈3.81 ms. Now add a 0.2 ms round trip per request. If each request waits for the previous one, 1,000×0.2=200 ms of latency dominates.

Allow 100 outstanding requests. In an idealized model there are ten rounds, so the latency component is 10×0.2=2 ms. The bytes still require 3.81 ms. Overlap means we cannot blindly add the two; time is at least their maximum before CPU work, contention, queues and other overhead.

With a warm 90% hit rate, only 100 pages go remote in this toy model. Comparing a warm old node with a cold new node would confound cache state and architecture.

Remote bytes halve but a chain of 100 dependent requests remains. Must time halve?

No. The serial request latency can remain dominant. Measure bytes, dependency depth, concurrent requests, queues and CPU separately; report cold transition and warm steady state.

sections.title: Multi-primary writes and recovery
sections.html:
Follow page P. Node A currently owns write authority at generation 7. Its cache changes P from 10 to 11 and creates log evidence. The durable page may still say 10. Before replying “commit,” the protocol must make its required log and commit evidence durable: write-ahead logging (WAL) separates durable evidence from delayed page writing.

A fails before flushing P. Recovery checks durable commit status and uses the log to reconstruct 11. It grants B current authority at generation 8. If A returns still believing generation 7 is valid, its old writes must be rejected. This rejection of obsolete authority is fencing. A network-partitioned owner can need fencing even while still alive.

Shared storage alone does not supply this protocol. A cached copy is not permission to write. Replicated old pages cannot recover a newer acknowledged value without the necessary evidence. With independent logs, locally increasing numbers alone may not give a sufficient cross-node replay order; interacting changes need declared ordering/dependencies.

A fails before commit evidence is durable. Must 11 survive as committed?

No. Recovery determines commit status using the protocol; an uncommitted change may be undone or ignored. Durable commit, page version and write authority answer separate questions. Acknowledging an update held only in volatile private memory would risk losing a promised change.

sections.title: Read two concrete multi-primary designs
sections.html:
Use the trace to read real designs. PolarDB-MP separates memory and storage; its PMFS service handles transaction visibility, shared buffers and locks, and the paper describes log ordering and recovery. It is a SIGMOD 2024 industrial paper in the Companion, not a PODS paper or SIGMOD research-track paper.

GaussDB also separates compute, memory and storage. Its memory layer manages global buffers/locks; page ownership, placement and routing help reduce transfers. Compare where authority lives and what moves during contention rather than assuming the architectures are interchangeable.

Neon's linked 2022 architecture account separates compute, WAL safekeepers and page serving. Use it to identify durability responsibilities, not to infer current pricing, SLA or every present implementation detail. For each paper, redraw the path of one read, one committed write and one failure. That makes unfamiliar system names answer a question we already understand.

Sources for this section: PolarDB-MP (SIGMOD 2024 Industry); GaussDB (PVLDB 2024); Neon’s official architecture account. Numerical traces marked original are teaching examples, not reported measurements.

sections.title: Mini-experiment: isolate the benefit and the network cost
sections.html:
An accessible experiment can isolate remote access rather than rebuild a production database. Compare local access, remote access without caching, and remote access with a fixed cache budget. Use sequential and random requests, then vary working-set size and skew. Sweep assumed latency separately from bandwidth; record latency distribution, throughput, bytes, cache hits, CPU and concurrency.

For a multi-writer prototype, increase hot-page contention and count ownership transfers, aborts/retries and coordination time. In a disposable sandbox, crash compute after durable commit but before page flush; verify committed values and measure recovery. A toy test does not certify high availability.

Separate fixed-total-resource scale-out from experiments adding memory/CPU. A single-machine delay model tests a mechanism, not RDMA, CXL or production control planes. H100s do not replace the CPU, storage and network resources needed here. State the narrow claim your available environment can actually test.

sections.title: Exercises and synthesis
sections.html:
Return to the opening failure. To preserve an acknowledged update, identify durable evidence, commit status, valid page version and current write authority. Independent resource scaling rearranges their costs without removing these requirements.

A new node doubles cache capacity and throughput rises 1.6×. What does this establish?

It establishes that measured combined change, not architectural efficiency alone. Compare equal total memory, disclose CPU/network differences, use a working set exceeding the original cache, and measure cold transition as well as steady state.

Storage is replicated. Is compute recovery unnecessary?

No. Copies may contain old pages. Recovery still needs the right durable evidence, commit decision, ownership/version rules, replay and fencing. Test the failure path separately from peak throughput.

Key takeaway

A useful cloud-native evaluation includes transitions and failures, not only steady-state peak throughput.

quiz.question: What does compute-storage disaggregation alone guarantee?
options: Linear scaling with compute nodes.
A separation of resource roles; other guarantees need explicit protocols.
No need for concurrency control.
Zero cold-start overhead.
quiz.explanation: Disaggregation is an architectural separation. Scalability, correctness, recovery and latency depend on mechanisms and workload.
quiz.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: In a simplified remote-page model, what is a risk of issuing many dependent requests serially?
options: Bandwidth becomes infinite.
Latency accumulates even when total bytes are modest.
Caches can no longer exist.
All reads become writes.
questions.explanation: Serial dependency chains pay repeated request latency. Reducing bytes alone may not fix that bottleneck.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: Why can scaling out compute cause a temporary slowdown?
options: Disaggregation forbids any caching.
All persistent data must always be deleted first.
Adding compute guarantees a slower network by definition.
New compute nodes may have cold caches and trigger additional remote access.
questions.explanation: Cold caches and state/ownership transitions can affect the scale-out period. They must be measured separately from steady state.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: A node acknowledges commit before its only log copy reaches durable storage, then loses volatile memory. What may fail?
options: Only the chart colors.
The definition of a vector embedding.
Durability of acknowledged work.
No property, because storage is remote.
questions.explanation: Commit acknowledgment must meet the system’s durable-commit protocol. Remote storage alone does not preserve information never durably recorded.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: Does a one-machine delay simulation reproduce a production RDMA/CXL database?
options: No; it can test a narrow model, but hardware and distributed-protocol claims require additional evidence.
No simulation can ever be useful.
Yes, if the simulation uses a GPU.
Yes, whenever the simulated delay matches one measured number.
questions.explanation: A model can isolate a mechanism while omitting bandwidth contention, hardware semantics, failures and control-plane behavior. State that boundary.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question
